analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates full public campaign funding if they qualify through small-dollar contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 40 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, but never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any House candidate opt into public financing. To qualify, a candidate would collect $5 contributions from voters in their state — 1,500 for major-party candidates — and then receive public funds for the primary and general elections instead of private donations, including extra public money if a privately funded opponent or outside groups outspent them. It also gave participating candidates free and discounted broadcast time, curbed unlimited party spending, tightened reporting of independent expenditures, and made the Federal Election Commission stronger and faster to act.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates without personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. A candidate could run a fully funded campaign by building support from small donations, rather than courting large contributors. The bill's own findings state the goal of ending the dominance of monied interests and making House races more competitive, since large donors historically give most of their money to incumbents.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates could qualify for public financing by collecting $5 qualifying contributions — 1,500 for major-party candidates and 150% of that threshold for others — and would then be barred from taking private money, receiving public funds instead for each election period.

If a privately funded opponent or independent spenders outspent a clean money candidate beyond 125% of their public allocation, the candidate would automatically receive matching public funds, capped at 200% of the base allocation.

Participating candidates would receive 30 minutes of free broadcast time in primary periods and 75 minutes in the general election, plus broadcast ad rates capped at 50% of the lowest rate in the run-up to elections.

The bill capped party committee spending in races involving a clean money candidate, required 24-to-48-hour reporting of independent expenditures and of private-money candidates' spending, and treated coordinated expenditures as contributions — closing routes through which outside money could overwhelm a publicly funded candidate.

It restructured the FEC with six presidentially appointed commissioners plus one nominated by the commission itself, added random post-election audits, gave the agency power to seek injunctions and expedite cases before elections, and mandated electronic filing.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would fund the new House of Representatives Election Fund through appropriations. Broadcasters would give up airtime and sell ads at reduced rates. Political party committees would face new spending caps in participating races. Large donors and incumbents' fundraising networks would lose their main channel of influence over House campaigns.

drawbacks.text: The program would be paid for by federal appropriations, adding a new taxpayer-funded election fund, though the bill's findings argue this is small against the cost of policy outcomes shaped by contributor access.

Clean money candidates could accept up to $35,000 in seed money and would lose the ability to raise unlimited small donations through normal channels, and self-funded wealthy candidates who stay outside the system could still spend freely, relying on the matching-funds trigger to keep pace.
Broadcasters would be required to provide free airtime and steep ad discounts, a direct regulatory cost that broadcasters have historically opposed.

The qualifying threshold of 1,500 contributions and tight spending caps could disadvantage candidates in large, expensive media markets relative to the historical spending averages used to set the base funding amount.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public cost is a modest line item compared with what the bill's sponsors argued is the larger hidden cost of a privately financed Congress: policy outcomes shaped by contributor access. The strongest good-faith objection is design, not principle — spending caps and matching funds have historically struggled to keep publicly funded candidates competitive against wealthy self-funded opponents and unregulated outside spending, and the bill's tight qualifying rules could deter some candidacies. Still, the core bargain — public funding in exchange for rejecting private money — directly addresses the influence of large donors over House elections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 31 original cosponsors and referred to three House committees, then to a subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the bill on June 28, 2005, joined by 31 original cosponsors including Rep. Bernie Sanders, an independent.
The Speaker referred it to the House Administration, Energy and Commerce, and Government Reform committees for consideration of provisions within their jurisdictions.
On July 29, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet of the House Administration Committee; that was the last action ever taken on it.
By the end of the Congress it had 40 cosponsors — 39 Democrats and 1 independent — and no Republican, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

The full text laid out the financing mechanics: $5 qualifying contributions, a House of Representatives Election Fund, public allocations set from the average spending of recent winning candidates, matching funds against outside spending, free broadcast time, reduced ad rates, party spending limits, and FEC restructuring.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing private-money system stayed fully intact. Large donors, incumbent fundraising operations, and political parties kept their current role in House campaigns, and broadcasters avoided the mandated free airtime and discounted rates. Ordinary voters lost their chance at a small-donor-based alternative to private campaign financing.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and wealthy households
industries.note: Clean money candidates would be barred from accepting private contributions beyond small qualifying and seed-money donations, cutting large donors out of House races in which opponents opted in. The bill's findings describe large contributors as having disproportionate influence over legislation.

Stations would have to give clean money candidates free airtime (up to 75 minutes in a general election) and cap campaign ad charges at 50% of the lowest rate, a direct revenue cost, in exchange for the public's benefit of candidate access to the airwaves.
Party spending in a race involving a clean money candidate would be capped at 10% of that candidate's public allocation, limiting parties' ability to flood districts with money.

Candidates funded by public money could not retain private fundraising, shrinking the market for fundraising consulting in participating races; the bill also tightened rules treating coordinated spending with consultants as a contribution.

Incumbents would gain access to public funding but lose two structural advantages: the fundraising edge that large donors give incumbents over challengers, and most franked (taxpayer-subsidized) mass mailings during election periods.
